It would publish to the world that there is something unsuitable in the conditions of Canada for the manufacture of iron and steel, and besidesit would give to that imfamous cad, Carnegie, an opportunity of boasting that he had sized up the iron conditions in Canada better than any other. I call him a cad advisedly, because I do not fancy the fellow can either read or write or has the slightest training, for if he had, he would not be guilty of the low and offensive remarks he made with reference to Canada.
When these bounties were announced some days ago, I thought they were adopted to improve the condition of the iron industry of Sydney. I understood that they would not assist the iron industry of Londonderry to any considerable extent which is not engaged in the manufacture of the particular class of iron protected by theses bounties. But these indstries do not want bounties. Why do we indulge in that unscientific way of helping industries ? I find that last year we imported from the United States $25,000,000 worth of the manufactured products of iron. What the iron industries of Londonderry and Sydney want is to be making and selling those products in Canada and getting that $25,000,000 which we now send to the United States. After depriving the manufacturers of this country of the home market, with which no other market is ^comparable, these hon. gentlemen tell them to go and compete with the foreign manufacturer in the markets of the United States or England or Germany. That is a poor compensation for the loss of their market at home. It must be an aggravating thing for a man who manufactures in this country to go to Montreal or Toronto to sell his goods, and find there some Yankee stealing away the markets of his country, which he
has helped to make. It is one of the basest betrayals a government was ever guilty of to force the manufacturers of this country to see their own markets stolen from them, and then to tell them to go and see what chance they have in foreign markets. Well, we have to take this dribble, and I take it without thanks ; I take it as not worthy of thanks. But I suppose that until * a great wholesome sentiment is created in this country, strong enough to sweep away these gentlemen, we will not do better.	But if I judge
the signs aright, I warn these gentlemen that the deluge is at hand, and that the whole manufacturing interests of Canada are not going to be imperilled to give these fourteen or fifteen gentlemen high offices. I would rather let them get out, and give my share to maintain them all their lives with splendid pensions and put in a government that will advance the interests of Canada. I fancied that the day was gone when a minister could call on his supporters to sustain him, no matter what liis principles were, and no matter how much he was injuring the great interests of the country. The Finance Minister should have said : ' I have been wrong in my political teaching ; in my early days I was a pupil of Alfred Jones, of Halifax, one of the narrowest men who has ever lived in the Dominion, or in any other part of the world ; my young mind was moulded by this man before it was able to stand alone, and I should not be judged for my errors, because they are an inheritance.' If the hon. gentleman would say that, I would say to him : ' If you Intend in future to do right, accept absolution, not only from myself, but from the Liberal-Conservative party, which has always been generous in forgiving its bitterest foes.' 1 saw in a Montreal paper the other day the statement by some gentleman that he had the assurance from the government of Canada-he did not say from whom-that in the near future a tariff would be submitted that would amply and sufficiently protect the iron industries of this country- I do not know whether that statement was made with authority or not; but I saw it, and was glad to see it, because I thought in some way it was inspired. But if the Minister of Finance will get up and say : ' We have sinned, but we intend to do better-because it is human to err, and it is God-like to reform and get on a higher platform-and we will give you the bounties to-day as a temporary measure, but before next session we will seek the assistance of experts and will give ample protection to the great iron industry of Canada, which will give this country character and wealth in the coming years.

The hon. Minister of Finance has answered the statement I made in a very peculiar way. I quoted the prices of articles which are protected in this country to the extent of 30 or 35 per cent. I have

shown by those prices that the theory which we hear so often that when there is a high tariff prices are high, is false. My hon. friend answers me :by calling my attention to the fact that in the United States these articles, which are protected there to about the same extent, sell at a little higher price. My hon. friend knows the condition of things in the United States ; he knows that wages are higher, the prices of farm products are higher, so much so that during the last five years they have increased in value 49 per cent, and everything else is higher. But that does not prove the contrary of my statement. When an article is sufficiently protected, there is enough competition to ensure reasonable prices. I expected somewhat the answer my hon. friend has given me, and I was prepared for it ; I know his trend of thought. My hon. friend would perhaps like to know what happens when there is no duty at all. I have proved that when we have sufficiently protected our manufacturers they are able to sell cheaper than their American competitors. Now, let me quote the prices during the past year of No. 9, No. 12 and No. 13 wire, which are free of duty. They are not manufactured here ; we do not manufacture a pound of them. What was the result ? It was very clear, because all the wire consumed in Canada is manufactured and sold by the Americans. They have two prices, one for their own citizens and another for Canadians. The price of No. 9 was $2.G0 in the United States and $2.85 in Canada ; No. 12 was $2.75 in the United States and $3 in Canada ; and No. 13 was $2.85 in the United States and $3.10 in Canada. In other words, when they have slaughtered one of our industries, they charge our people more than they do their own citizens. And we are pleased with that state of affairs ; and because I happen to share the views of those who do not believe in a policy which has that result, venerable men like my hon. friend from Victoria (Hon. Mr. Boss) lecture me. He invites me to remember that some of my hon. friends on the other side of the House were some time ago saying a lot of hard things about me. A lot of things have been said about me during the last thirty years that I have been a newspaper man. I was not killed by those weapons, I am still alive, and I do not care much what is said about me, when I am sure I do not deserve any censure. My hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gourley) has alluded once more to what he calls my Paris speeches. He read them in the English language. I am sorry he is not a French scholar.
I will read them in French.

I invite him to read them in French and not in distorted reports in English, and I say without hesitation that they might have been made by any English citizen sitting in parliament. This little Hon. Mr. TARTE.
incident being closed, let me say only one word more. When there is a sufficient Canadian tariff, we are able to compete with our American friends and neighbours. We are able to sell to our own customers as cheap as, if not cheaper than they sell to their citizens. The reasons are obvious. They have a condition of affairs which does not exist here. There, wages are higher and the cost of living higher. We have everything here necessary to build up large industries, to develop our cities, to furnish home markets to our farmers, and we are doing none of these things. When my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was asking me to believe that a high tariff increases prices, I was very nearly getting up and begging the hon. Minister of Customs to come to my rescue without any delay, because he has allowed-and I am equally responsible with him-an increase in the duties on several things. Let us take cement, he has increased the duty on cement. What has been the result ? Several new factories have sprung up and we are manufacturing first-class cement. We are manufacturing it more and more. What is true of cement is true of everything else.

My hon. friend gave us some interesting figures a few moments ago, which seemed to bring out very clearly some important facts showing the effect of a high tariff. He has now added to that information something equally important. He has quoted facts in connection with the wire industry, and has shown that the manufacturers of wire in the United States are charging excessively high prices for that article. He has thus proved that in an industry probably protected to the extent of fifty per cent or sixty per cent or seventy per cent, in the United States, the manufacturers are able, through the operation of a high tariff, to create monopolies, trusts and combines, which enable them to dictate prices to their customers.

My hon. friend knows political history better than that. He cannot ignore that there are more monopolies in free trade England than in the United States. When a free trader is put to the wall by a sound argument, he is able to do anything.

What is desired is to give immediate relief to the iron industry, and the question for us to consider is whether this bounty is more likely to be of immediate benefit to that industry than would be an increased duty. The point to decide is whether an equal amount of bounty in money will assist the manufacturers as well as an equal amount derived from a protective duty. Let us suppose that the manufacturer makes his iron or steel as cheaply as he can, he will have in addition a bounty which will enable him to compete with any other producer. On the other hand, if I

understood my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, he said that a duty would create greater competition and consequently reduce prices. But our object is to give the manufacturers a higher price or more money; and if you reduce the price at which he sells his article, he is losing money. What then must he do V He cannot reduce the prices of the raw material or the machinery, and he will have to fall back on his unfortunate labourers and reduce the wages paid them. That is one of the effects of the custom system. The bounty gives immediate relief to the manufacturer, and behind that is the question which will benefit the customer the most. But as the question before us now is the giving of immediate aid to the manufacturers, that aid will be most readily given through the bounty system.

As there are iron industries of importance right in my county, I am not disposed to warmly congratulate the government oh the assistance given this particular industry, although I am glad for the parties concerned that their important industry has been saved from distress. I do not think however that the system adopted by the present government will have any effect in the way of protecting, as should be done, the great iron industry, which is the basic industry of this country. If we wish to preserve that very important industry in our midst, we will have to follow the example of the countries which have created it among themselves. We will have to follow the example of Germany, Belgium and the United States, whose tariff has been prepared with the greatest care-with such care in fact that it enables that country to dominate us completely in the production of iron. My hon. friend from St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has referred to the wire industry. We in the county of Jacques Cartier, before the elections of 1896, had an excellent manufactory which produced numbers nine, twelve and thirteen wire. These three were drawn and were excellent wire, and moreover, that important manufactory produced nearly the whole barb wire required in this country. What happened ? My hon. friends, in conformity with what they preached on every hustings before 1896, when they declared that we were paying exorbitant prices for barb wire and that the duties should be abolished, carried out their policy in the tariff of 1897.
The consequence was that we became dependent on American producers for products of iron and steel. The barbed wire factory at Lachine had to give up the manufacture of barbed wire, and for No. 9, No. 12 and No. 13 wire, we became dependent upon the Americans. As a result, we have dearer barbed wire since, and wire of inferior quality, as everybody knows and we are entirely under the control of the
American industrials for that wire. It is humiliating to hear it mentioned in this House that 26,000 tons of wire were imported into this country last year. It is humiliating to think that over $30,000,000 of iron products were brought into this country last year. As a matter of fact it is well known the Americans import from here steel and iron ingots upon which they pay $6 a ton duty, and, after they have manufactured them into all sorts of articles, they sell them tack to us. The manufacture of these ingots is carried on in bond, and the manufacturers get a rebate of $5.99 per ton when the material is sent back to this country in a manufactured state. That is the condition of affairs in my own county ; and, without having had occasion to consult these very important manufacturers who have invested millions in this industry, that they have developed in the county of Jacques Cartier, I question very much whether in the case of the great factory that used to manufacture wire and barbed wire and has been obliged to confine its operation to the manufacture of steel nails, depending entirely upon the American manufacturers for wire, this resolution will benefit them in any way. The fact is that it is generally claimed by those well acquainted with this industry that what we require is a remodelling of our duties in such a way as to protect every line of production, because new lines have arisen in the past ten years. If we wish to make that industry our own and not be dependent on the Americans-who would never for a single instant be dependent upon us for such a production-we must remodel the duties from end to end. Only then shall we become, in respect to this industry, a really independent people. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has spoken of the higher prices in the United States. It is well known that the reason of that is the existence in the United States of these immense trusts, combinations that, not content to control the prices in the United States, tyrannize over us in Canada in regard to these prices. We are the slaves, in respect to certain articles, of these gigantic trusts of the United States. As an example-and many others might be given- it is sufficient to point out what condition our tobacco growers and our tobacco merchants are reduced to at the present time through the dominating influence of the American trust. In the province of Quebec that trust is doing incalculable harm to the manufacturers, who cannot resist its influence, and even to the tobacco growers. Anybody who wishes to convince himself of the truth of what I have -said has only to read the report of Judge MacTavish, who was charged by the government with the duty of investigating this subject. It has become necessary for the government, in order to protect the tobacco growers of our province and of the province of Ontario, actual-

ly to introduce an amendment .to the Criminal law, to free us to a certain extent, from the domination of these American invaders of our country. What has been never explained to me, and what I can never understand, is why, in the matter of bounty-to my mind, though a convinced protectionist, a most disastrous system of protection-a difference is made between the producers of iron and those engaged in other lines of industry. Why is it, for instance that the cotton manufacttirers, who are afflicted with the British preference, are not aided at the present juncture in the same way as the iron producers are aided ? Why is it that the woollen manufacturers, who have suffered great injury by the present state of the tariff, and particularly by the British preference, they who have been, in many instances known to horn members in this House, forced to close their manufactories, are not assisted ? Why is it, for instance, I would ask the Minister of Finance, that the producers of paper in this country are not assisted in this way ? If it is impossible to come to their relief by changes in the paper duty, by which we could not only give to these producers the markets of this country, but give them great influence in the markets of the world, why is it that they are not assisted by bounties, since we are obliged to resort to the pis-aller in the way of assistance to certain producers ? Throughout the province of Quebec-X do not speak of Ontario, though 1 believe that there analogous conditions exist-we have untold wealth of pulp wood. But through the treacherous policy of our provincial government our pulp wood lauds are depleted, and our pulp wood is sent to the United States to be manufactured into paper and sold back to us, the whole profit going to American workmen and to American capitalists. Yet my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, if I mistake not, less than a year ago reduced the duty on certain classes of paper, thereby giving still greater advantage to the American industrials. We are the laughing stock of the great American industrials in this respect. Has my hon. friend the Minister of Finance read the very able exposition of his case by Mr. McGibbon, manager, I believe, of the great pulp mills of Shawinigau ? The conclusion at which he arrives, and which is absolutely irrefutable, is that if we had a proper policy with regard to that line of industry, befoi'e ten years the Americans would- construct over $100,000,000 worth of factories throughout Canada, and would be paying more than $4,000,000 a year- in wages" to our Canadian workmen, instead of the whole profit of that industry being taken by American capitalists and American workmen. And so convinced are our American neighbours that eventually we will realize our position and carry out a more patriotic policy in this respect that, as Mr. McGibbon points out, they are purchasing

our best water-powers. They are preparing for the time, which they feel wall come before long, when, if they want to manufacture, deprived as they are of pulp wood in their own country, they can come into Canada and establish the factories which Mr. McGibbon tells us they would already establish if a wise policy were carried out by our government.

The hon. Minister of Finance referred to the trusts of the United States, and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has also spoken of these great combinations. The bounty system of the European continental nations, such as Germany, Belgium, and France applied to the item of sugar has wiped out the sugar refineries of Great Britain. The manufacturers of this country, a great proportion of them at least, are just as thoroughly under the influence of the great American trusts-and will he more so as time goes on-as the British sugar refiners were under the Influence of the bounty fed sugar of continental Europe. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier referred to a certain industry in his constituency which got its raw material in the shape of wire for the manufacture of wire nails from the American trust. I should not he surprised, nor, I suppose, would the proprietor of that institution-though I am not more familiar with the circumstances of the case than I have learned from my hon. friend-If that proprietor were to find on his desk some morning a letter from the trust in the United States, who are supplying him 'with wire, to say that the trust had made up their mind to advance the price of wire, or, even, in the future, themselves to supply the Canadian trade with wire nails.
I have myself seen letters of that kind from these American trusts, and I wish to say in this House that there is no body of men, not Including the government of the United States, that are so tyrannical in their methods of operation and so selfish as the United States trusts. It will he necessary for the government of this country, whether Liberal or Conservative, so to arrange our tariff that they will he able to defeat the objects of these wealthy and enormous United States trusts. I fancy that a good deal of pressure must have been brought to bear on the Finance Minister in regard to these iron and steel bounties. I cannot understand what different pressure . could have been brought to hear upon him than that which was brought to bear upon him from other industries in this country, .some of which have been mentioned. From the remarks of the hon. gentleman the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) I should take it for granted that so far as he was concerned he expected that the government in future would deal with the tariff on the bounty basis. If that Is the case, I do not see how they are going to carry out any

such policy. I believe, as others have said, that it is a piecemeal policy ; more than that, it is uncertain and indefinite. We want an adequate protective tariff in this country, a stable tariff, so that people will know what thev have to calculate against so far as European and United States competition are concerned.
What I have to complain about more especially is the indefinite position of the government in regard to this bounty question. In 1897, the Minister of Finance, in introducing his budget, and in changing the tariff to some extent, gave his views in regard to fiscal questions, and he laid down certain principles upon which we expected that he intended to be guided in the future.
It seems to me, as it must appear to every member of this House, that he does not entertain the same views in the year 1903 that he did in 1897, and I hope for the good of the country that he will continue to entertain different views from those of 1897. He was very severe upon the manufacturers of this country. Who are the manufacturers of this country ? Where does the money come from that the manufacturing industries are carried on with ? I have heard it stated on good authority, on the authority of a supporter of the hon. gentleman opposite, who is a manufacturer and well posted, that three-quarters of the capital invested in manufacturing industries in this country is borrowed capital. The manufacturer is there to defend his calling, to pay 100 cents on the dollar, and to pay his banker, or whoever he borrows the money from, a proper rate of interest. Now, upon this bounty question the Minister of Finance appears to have had, the session before last, entirely different ideas from those he has to-day. In 1901 he did not appear to be under the impression that this government would in future adopt an extension of the bounty system. Let us call the attention of the committee to a debate which took place in 1901, introduced by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Morrison). That hon, gentleman, in the course of his remarks, said this :
What I wish to draw the attention of the government to is this, that the Dominion of Canada stands !fco pay out a very large amount of money in the way of bounties, and I would like to know whether it is too late for the government to take such steps as may, while not invading any vested rights, at the same time prevent further vested interests growing up under the Act.
The Finance Minister in the course of his answer, said :
There is that comfort to us in the first place. There is the further comfort that even if this system should result in the payment of large sums of money, that payment will speedily come to an end, because at the very time we provided the scale of bounties, we stated that it was regarded by us as of vital importance that the bounties should be gradually reduced by tihe terms of the Act itself ; so that after a term
of five years, beginning on the 1st of July next, the bounties will cease to exist. If, therefore, for a short time we should be called upon to pay even a large sum for the development of these industries, we would have the comfort of knowing in the meantime that as a result of that experiment there must grow up a vast amount of business in tihe Dominion which would not probably have grown up except for that development ; and that If the bounty should he large, it can only continue for five years, when it will be wiped off the statute-book.
Now, it appears to me, Mr. Chairman, that this government are not only uncertain in regard to the tariff, but they are uncertain in regard to the bounties, and in regard to tlie whole fiscal question. The government this session have dealt with specific items in tlie tariff, with binder twine, lead and steel, and in regard to all these they have dealt witli them upon a bounty basis. I have watched with some interest the remarks of the Finance Minister when dealing with these questions ; and I do not know whether other hon. gentlemen have noticed it or not, but I have noticed that he is very careful bow be uses the word ' protection.' In fact he scarcely ever uses that word. I noticed that in referring to the steel rail question, or the protection on steel rails which the Governor in Council was empowered to make, he referred to that, not as protecting the steel rail industry, but be called it tariff encouragement. .Tust think of having to use two words to express one word. Protection is an old, well known word, but he would not use the word ' proiection.' He uses tlie phrase tariff encouragement enjoyed by other industries. The hon. gentleman also, in apologizing for protection, used the words : ' Approach the subject with moderation;' ' approach the subject with caution;'
' the government desire to avoid extremes;'
* they wish stability in the tariff.' Now all this is intended no doubt to appeal to the electorate. But that does not meet tlie situation which exists to-day, and which is bound to exist in the future. Have we not arrived at the time when we must have an adequate protective policy in this country? The Minister of Finance, in introducing his budget this year, said that we must watch how our opponents played the game. It did seem to me that he was just then balancing himself, uncertain whether lie ought to become a protectionist or remain as lie was in the past, a sort of free-trade-protectionist- I do not know what not. Now I would like to draw Ills attention to this fact, that our opponents are practically playing the game to-day the same as they have played it for many years past. They are playing it to-day the same as they were playing it in 1897, and it is the false theories of lion, gentlemen opposite that have been knocked out. Our opponents are playing the same game in regard to the tariff that they have played for many years past. Now, Mr. Chairman, I I would "like to say that I do not think this

bonus or bounty system is tile proper one, I do not think any one can defend it. Here we are trying to give a bonus to all these different articles :
Angles, tees, channels, beams, joists, girders cr bridge, building or structural rolled sections, and on other rolled shapes not round, oval, square or flat, -weighing not less than thirty-five pounds per lineal yard and also on flat eye bar blanks, when sold for consumption in Canada a bounty ot $3 per ton.
It seems to me that we cannot follow up this thing, that the government are going to become a sort of partners, or agents to investigate the business of these people, and it is a wrong principle. What I plead for is a. decided policy on the part of the government. It is necessary at present in order that every one may know what it is, and that any one may safely go into an industry knowing that it is adequately protected. Belore I resume my seat I wish to say that in the absence of adequate protection on these iron and steel products I approve of these bounties which have been granted to the steel industry. They will be of use to them, and will assist to some extent in maintaining their operations and building up the iron industry which we must maintain at all hazards.

By granting these bounties a certain specified object is accomplished, and I therefore can-aot agree with ^ lion, gentlemen opposite in the view that it is an unwise proceeding. They say that they -would have proceeded by way of a revision of the tariff. By granting these bounties "we will give encouragement, if I may use that word, to this industry, we will secure the manufacture of those goods in this country which heretofore we have not produced. I think that we have the proof that it will bring about that end, and therefore, instead of viewing these propositions as ineffective, I think they will prove amply effective and more effective than if it had been done by way of a tariff revision. The works, as I understand it, that are to produce, these articles are about to expend $1,500,000 for machinery and plant for that purpose. That expenditure made, the articles will without doubt be produced in this country and they will be for sale in this country and afford as tliey will the raw material of numbers of manufacturers employing in the aggregate I venture to say, many times over the number of men that will be employed in this concern, and these manufacturers will not be burdened in the production of goods thalj they are now producing and confer a benefit upon the workingmen, and confer a benefit upon the whole country. This [DOT]we are accomplishing in this wire rod business, for instance. When the tariff was revised it was considered wise as these rods were not produced in this country and as they were the raw material of other

manufacturers employing a great number of men, to place them on the free list, with the result that the farmer who formerly paid $1 a keg duty upon his wire nails, now gets them at 60 cents a keg duty, or a 40 per cent reduction upon nails. Wire rods will be made in this country by the aid of the bounty, which will not increase the price of the wire rod by one cent to the wire drawer or to the manufacturer of nails. Whatever may he said in reference to whether it would be better to aid this industry by way of a bonus or tariff the question under consideration now is : Is this a wise step that we are taking? Are we going to get results from it ? I think hon. gentlemen opposite know from what they can gather from the newspapers that we shall have an established manufacture of these lines of goods of which there were large importations, that we will effect the manufacture of them in this country and that we will not burden the scores if not hundreds of other manufacturers employing not only thousands, but tens of thousands of men who use these products as their raw material and without burdening by one iota the consumer, who will get his goods just as cheaply as before. That is the proposition that is before us. I do not intend to enter into an argument as to the relative merits of protection or free trade.
Who pays the bounty ?

The community in general pay the bounty. There is no doubt about that. I shall not enter into that argument. I only want to ask hon. gentlemen opposite who are adopting a pessimistic tone that is calculated to affect the stability and spirit that is in our people : What industries are there in the country that are not thriving at the present time ? What industries are languishing ?
Woollens.

Woollens are not languishing. The hon. gentleman must not hold the government policy responsible for keeping every manufacturing industry on its feet. Because some industries in certain lines do not pay you cannot hold us responsible. If there are other industries and other men employed in producing the same line of goods making money and paying large dividends, the failure of one industry is not due to the tariff, but must be due to some other cause. I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to point me out a single manufacturing line In Canada in which some men are not making goods-and making them at a profit to themselves ?

I do not wish to oppose these resolutions, but in view of a great deal that has been said to-day, I do not think it would be fair to the interests which I represent if I allowed the discussion to end without giving expression to the opinions which I hold, and which I believe are held by a very large proportion of the people of this country in rgard to the subject under' discussion. In presenting these views, it is desirable to place certain facts which do not seem to be generally known before the House and before the country. The discussion that has taken place in regard to the iron industry to-day and on previous occasions in the House, has proceeded under the assumption that the industry of producing iron and the separate industry of manufacturing iron are practically without the protection of import duties in Canada at the present time. It will surprise some people to know that to-day scrap iron pays a duty of one dollar a ton, pig-iron $2.50 a ton and steel ingots $2 a ton. That is the duty, truly it is only a revenue duty, but it gives the industry of producing iron that measure of protection. Then, after the iron has been produced ; in the first stage of its manufacture, which merely consists of plain casting or the production of malleable iron in some form, I find that rolled iron not less than 35 pounds weight per yard has a protective duty-we can only call it a protective duty-of $7 a ton ; bar iron or steel less than 8 inches wide and less than one-half inch thick has a duty of $7 per ton ; iron or steel plates less than 30 inches wide, $7 a ton ; railway fish plates, $8 a ton ; steel rails other than the rails of steam railways, 30 per cent; cast iron pipes, $8 per ton ; switches, frogs, &c., for railways, 30 per cent; steel castings in the rough, 25 per cent; stove plates, surely not an article that requires any great amount of labour in their production-25 per cent; cart or wagon skeins-a plain casting-30 per cent. I would like to know what that part of the industry which relates to the production of iron, and much more that part of the industry which relates to the manufacture of iron in its cruder form-I would like to know what these industries want. If they are not satisfied with the duty that is levied on the production of iron and the bounty that is given in addition to that duty, then certainly there must be something wrong with the iron industry in this country. It must then be the wrong country in which to enter into this industry, and it is better for the country at large, better for the manufacturing industry which depends on cheap iron, better for the agricultural industry, which depends very largely on cheap iron, better for the transportation industry, both on land and water, which essentially depends on
cheap iron ; it is better for these industries and for the country at large that the iron required for these industries should be imported rather than be manufactured in Canada. This is the wrong place for an iron industry, if that iron industry cannot thrive under the conditions which prevail at the present time. I have said before in this House, and I take the liberty of repeating it, that in Canada cheap iron is as essential to the welfare and the prosperity of the country as is cheap food to the manufacturing industries of England. AVe must have cheap iron or we cannot do business. On that point-just referring for a moment to the fancy picture drawn by the member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) as to what would be the result if we increased the cost of raw iron to our agricultural, manufacturing and transportation interests ; and the tide of prosperity that would flow over this country-let me refer the House to the condition of affairs in this country when there was so-called adequate protection to this very iron industry. Where was the flood of prosperity at that time ? What was the actual and absolute and necessary and unquestioned result of these high duties on iron at that time ? It was the paraliza-tion practically of the greater part of our manufacturing industry, even though it also had high protective duties. If this were merely a matter of theory, if it were something that was in prospect, we might admit the arguments that have been put forward to-day ; but when we have had a sad experience of these high iron duties, I cannot understand the propriety of the arguments that are put forward in favour of repeating the mistake that was made in those past years.
As to the question of bounties, and as to the difference between bounties and duties, some of our friends object to bounties because they are merely an expedient. My objection to the resolution now before the House is not because it is a bounty, or because as a bounty it is an expedient, but because it is not an expedient but a policy if carried to its legitimate and logical conclusion, according to the statements that have been made here to-day by the Minister of Finance, by the member for St. Mary's and by other speakers. Let me point out the difference between bounties as applied to the production of iron, and bounties as applied to the manufacture of . iron. A bounty given for the production of iron is in itself an expedient; it is supported because it is an expedient and only because it is an expedient. Our condition in this country is that we have vast quantities of iron ore and vast quantities of coal. It must be evident then that if we can bring the iron and the coal together under such conditions as will permit us to produce raw iron profitably, a vast industry will be created in this country to the benefit of every one in the country. The con-

ditions are not, however, absolutely favourable. The coal is in one place and the iron is in another, and the experiment of bringing them together can only be undertaken at very considerable expense, and with a chance of very considerable loss. It is an experiment which capitalists may be slow to undertake. The government then comes forward and says : We will take an interest in this experiment, we will provide a system of bounties which will help to enable you to undertake this experiment; we will stand part of the loss. If the experiment proves that in Canada we can bring together profitably the iron and the coal in order to produce raw iron on the merits of the enterprise itself, then our money has been well expended and your industry may go on and thrive on its own merits. That is the principle as 1 understand it underlying the granting of bounties on the production of raw iron, and those bounties are scaled down from year to year so that after the experiment has had reasonable opportunities, if it turns out to be a success the bounties cease, and also if it turns out a failure the bounties cease. The capitalists who desired to invest in that industry are having their opportunity, and are having their' assistance, and if success is attained, so much the better. There is nothing wrong in this principle. It is a common sense principle. It has nothing whatever to do with the principle of protection in connection with the tariff, and it will be observed that essentially and above everything it is an experiment ; it is an expedient.
But the system of bounties which we have at present, and which the present resolutions propose to extend for a short time, and very properly so possibly under the circumstances, is different altogether in principle and ultimate conclusion from the other feature which it is proposed to introduce, that is to say, a bounty for the manufacture of iron in the country after it has been produced. None of the reasons which apply to the bringing together of the coal and the ore to produce the iron apply to the manufacture of iron into its coarser and rawer forms after it has been once produced. Either we have skill and enterprise and capital which will enable us to install machinery and to run that machinery to work up this iron after we produce it, or we have not that skill, enterprise and capital. If we have not got it, then we cannot afford to buy it at the price of paying more for that iron than it is actually worth. We need too much iron in this country, we need it for too many essential purposes, to afford the price which it is apparently supposed that this iron is going to cost us. For my part, I claim that there is nothing in the conditions or the facts, as we know them, to warrant the conclusion that we cannot manufacture the iron in this country once it has been produced, at any rate, under a reasonable and moderate revenue tariff such as we have to-day. If we can Mr. OLIVER.
produce manufactured articles of the highest grade and quality, into which skill and industry and capital very largely enter, under the moderate protection of a revenue tariff, we certainly ought to be able to manufacture tlie coarser forms into which skill and energy do not enter nearly so largely as mere capital.
My view of this feature of the resolutions is this. We propose to give a bounty for the manufacture of steel wire, of heavy plates and of heavy structural iron. We import these articles very largely ; we need them very largely ; we must have them, or we cannot progress ; and I think the government are doing very wisely in not putting a duty upon these articles higher than the present duty. The one is free and the others are under the very moderate duty of 10 per cent. But the government's proposition, as it is placed before the House, is to give a bounty on the manufacture of these articles. There is no proposition to reduce that bounty from year to year, as in the case of the bounty ou the production of iron, so that it will pass out of existence by process of time. As the proposition stands, to my mind it is this. The offer is held out to manufacturers of iron to undertake the manufacture of these lines under the promise of the payment of a certain bounty. There is no indication that the bounty will at any future time be withdrawn. If those people purchase machinery and invest the capital necessary to enter upon these enterprises on the basis of the bounty that is given, I for one do not see very well how it would be fair or right to withdraw the bounty. Once we begin to pay it we must continue to pay it, or we are accused of unfairness to this investment of capital. So long as our manufacture of iron is small in proportion to our imports, it certainly pays better to give the bounty than to pay a higher duty. But so soon as our manufacture of iron increases till we are manufacturing more than we import, then it will be better for us to have a duty than to pay the bounty. It seems to me that is the natural and logical conclusion of the proposition now placed before the House. If it is right and proper to pay bounties and ultimately to pay duties on the manufacture of these classes of iron, of which I think it was stated that Canada now imports over $2,000,000 a year, there is no ground that I can see for not taking the same position in regard to other productions of iron ; and I feel the duty and responsibility resting upon me, as a representative in parliament, to say to the government and the House that I do not believe that that policy can be pursued to its legitimate conclusion without the greatest possible damage to the best interests of this country.
It appears to me, from the figures which I have taken from the blue-books, that this proposition involves a sort of double bounty in addition to the duty which we also pay

on the iron. We pay now, I believe, a bounty of $2.70 a ton on pig-iron, and there is besides a duty upon it of $2.50 a ton ; so that our producers of iron have an advantage over their competitors, exclusive of freight rates, of some $5.20 per ton on pig-iron and $4.70 on steel. Then, when this steel is turned into wire rods, and they acquire the additional bounty of $6 per ton, they are winners to the extent of $10.70 per ton on steel wire rods as against their competitors from other countries. That is to say, we are paying something like $10 a ton more for these steel rods than we can buy them for elsewhere. On the heavy plates and structural steel the duty and the bounty are the same as on the production of the iron, and the additional proposed bounty is $3 per ton.
That is $7.70 per ton of an advantage on heavy structural iron and heavy steel plates, that is to say, on steel bridges and the plates which go to the building of vessels and locomotives. It is a tax then on the transportation of the country in the matter of steel bridges and in the building of steamboats and locomotives. I consider that the necessities of this country with regard to transportation are such as do not warrant our imposing any such tax on those industries. The same remark applies to the manufacturing industry at large, into which iron and steel enter so largely.
I just want to say a word with regard to the subject of bounties for the production of iron. I 'consider that these bounties are based on sound principles. They are not excessive. It does not matter to us whether they are extended a year or two or shortened a year or two, if we can bring about the result we desire, namely, make Canada an iron producing country. But I find, on looking over the returns, that so far from the bounties we are paying having the effect of building up an iron producing industry in Canada and developing our own iron and coal mines, for every dollar of bounty we paid during the past year for the production of iron from Canadian ore, we paid $2 for the production of iron from foreign ore. Out of every $3 that we pay in bounties for the production of iron supposedly for the building up of an iron producing industry from our own ore in our own country, we pay $2 for the production of iron from ore which comes from a foreign country. We are, therefore, paying this money out to no purpose, so far as the building up of an iron producing industry in our own country is concerned. Here are the figures for the past year of the bounties paid respectively on Canadian ore and on foreign ore to the various smelters :
	Canadian Ore,	Foreign Ore.
*Midland	. .. $ 56,036	$ 24,109Radnor	. .. 15,580	2,722Deseronto.. .	. .. 611	21,920Sidney	347,436Hamilton..	39,795New Glasgow	.. .. 19,290	42,065$211,860	$478,047
That was for the year ending 30th June, 1902. For the year just closed, _the total bounties paid amounted to $1,245,382. I submit that while we should do our share in the attempt to produce iron in Canada from Canadian ore with Canadian coal, it is not a business proposition on our part to bonus to such a degree the production of the iron mines of foreign countries. If this is the sort of home industry which the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and lion, gentlemen opposite are so anxious to promote, I cannot see eye to eye with them. I do not think it is good policy to spend our money in such a way.
I am out for the development of the legitimate industries and natural resources of this country, and I do not care what you call the means you take to produce that development. You can call it protection or free trade, high tariff or bounty, but I want to see that when we spend our money we get the desired result. I want to see that when we pay out one and a quarter million dollars to build! up a Canadian iron industry, the money goes to build up that industry and not to the production of iron from foreign ores.
I do not know that it is necessary to say anything with regard to the fervid patriotism indulged in by the hon. member for St. Mary's division and other hon. members when endorsing a prospective policy of high duties. Canada for the Canadians is their motto. It is also mine. But I believe in Canada for all Canadians and not for only a section of them. That is the difference between their policy and mine. I believe in a policy that will build up legitimate, natural industres in this country, but not in a policy designed to make possible artificially, industries whch are not naturally possible. Such a policy is not a national policy, but a system of unjust taxation, unfair to the majority of the people and bound to result in any thing but the well-being of the country.

I want to say a word or two on this matter. Some hon. gentlemen on this side have expressed the hope that this is a measure which in the end will lead up to a legitimate measure of protection. If I entertained that view, I would probably take a somewhat different position from that which I propose to do. Had I any doubt about the matter, an incident of this afternoon would dispel it. I had the pleasure of hearing the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross) read the hon. member the ex-Minister of Pubic Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) out of the ranks of the Liberal party. That, to my mind, is a very significant point at this time in the course of the warfare between the Conservative and Liberal parties as to the tariff that we shall have in Canada. For we must bear in mind that the only point of difference between the government today and the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, so far as we know, at all events,

is the question of protection or no adequate protection to our industries. I do not think we can assume that so venerable, so experienced a gentleman as the hon. member for Victoria, Nova Scotia, and a gentleman in such close touch with the cabinet could take such a step without having instructions from the ministers of the crown as to the attitude he should take. It, therefore, seems perfectly plain to me, and I think the country will not be slow to take the intimation that although the government would like, perhaps, to have it go to the country for the time being, at least to certain sections, that they are going to stand by a policy of free trade, and to other sections, which interviewed them from time to time by deputations and otherwise, that they propose to introduce such amendments to the tariff as will afford adequate and reasonable protection to the industries of Canada, yet those who have been promised a fair and adequate measure of protection have no reason to hope that such promise will be implemented by the action of the government. I therefore think that those who have indulged the hope have given the government credit for too great a degree of sincerity; and, so far as their action in connection with the tariff and the policy they have enunciated from time to time lias enabled us to judge, I think we are not wise in coming to the conclusion that the country can expect any adequate relief so long as hon. gentlemen who at present administer the affairs of Canada are left in control. Now, the iron and steel industry is a most important industry to Canada, and I believe that the conditions of this country with regard to the quantity of raw material, the means of obtaining it, and the quality of that material when obtained, are such as to promise that we can develop a large and prosperous industry in this line of manufacture. Whatever will make for the success of that industry along legitimate lines, I am. perfectly prepared to support. But, as regard bounties, I do not feel that this is the means by which we can give encouragement to the iron industry along legitimate lines. The iron industry should be developed side by side with the other industries of the country. One should not profit at the expense of the other. And, when I venture to oppose, as I intend to oppose in toto, the resolution introduced this afternoon, I shall do so with the full knowledge that, more than any other single cause, Great Britain owes the proud position she occupies to-day to the development of her iron industry. I recognize too, that, for the time being, it looks as if supremacy in the iron trade had passed across the Atlantic and remained for the present with the United States. But I look to the time when the centre of gravity will change again, and when in this Dominion, with its vast re- 1 sources, with its energetic people and enor-1 Mr. LENNOX.
; mous territory, we shall develop an in-
[DOT]	dustry in iron and steel second to none in
[DOT]	the world. But, whilst I recognize this, I * am opposed to bounties on principle. In saying this, I have the sanction and approval of
; many prominent gentlemen on the government side of the House. I remember very 1 well how eloquent they were in denunciation of protection, but not so eloquent as they were in denuciation of bounties, describing bounties-or subventions as some called them-as the most odious form of protection. I do not think that we can, by means of bounties, develop the country upon the lines of protection as understood by the Conservative party. I believe bounties are necessarily unequal in their operation. If, for instance all our industries were bounty fed, none would be bounty fed. It is seen at a glance, if you commence to analyze the question, the' only conclusion that can be reached is that to give a bounty to every industry would be to tax every industry to raise that bounty, and so all would be on the same basis as before. But, to give bounties to some and not to others, must be detrimental to those that are not bounty fed. In other words, it is a means of robbing certain parties to give encouragement to the others. I submit, it is not a policy that we can safely or properly pursue in this country. It is more than this-it is a development of one section of the country at the expense of the others. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) referred to the question of bounties on raw material. I cannot at the moment recall the case of any industry which I would recommend the government to bonus. We had a question not long ago before this parliament of giving a bounty for the raising of the sugar beet. Perhaps, if there is any instance in which a bounty is justifiable, it could be better contended for in the case of a bounty which will lead to the production of raw material, because that is an enrichment to the country. If you delve into the bowels of the earth and bring up useful minerals of which the people previously knew nothing, you add so much to the wealth of the country. And, if that raw material cannot possibly be obtained except by the expenditure of some of the public money, perhaps there can be a reasonable argument advanced in support of the expenditure. And that argument applies with great force when the farmers of the country are approaching an experiment which it is hoped will lead to an industry for the benefit of the people as a whole. In such a case, there might be good excuse for considering and responding to their petition. But we find that the government refused to give them any relief at all. giving a miserable fraction of a cent, not to the farmers, not to the producers, not to those who made the raw material, but those who were in the case secondary parties in the transaction, the manufacturers.
I have heard it said this afternoon

that the bounty was a form of protection. I know that, speaking in a general way, without regard to exactness, perhaps even a Conservative might speak of bounty as a form of protection. I know that supporters of the government have been in the habit of speaking of it in that way. But I claim that a bounty is not in any reasonable sense protection of any kind. A bounty is merely the means of making a present to the manufacturer at the expense of the people at large. It creates no wealth in the country. It is a means of transferring money from the pocket of one man to the pocket of another ; it is a means of compelling the people generally to enhance the profits of the manufacturer, to put into his pocket money that he never earned. A bounty therefore is a means of impoverishing the country as a whole. Protection, on the other hand, is but a legitimate form of self defence, a means by which we may secure the home market for the people of Canada, a means by which we may build up industries and make ourselves self-sus-taiuing, a means by which we may increase the tangible wealth of the country and build up varied industries from one end of it to the other. If you want to ascertain whether a subvention or bonus does anything to add to the wealth of the country, take this illus-[DOT] tration. Let there be a bounty of $1,000,000 distributed among the various manufacturers, a bounty of $1,000,000 a year distributed for 100 years, and what is the result ? The result is that you have paid out $100,000,000 of the money of the people of Canada, and I ask you, although you have made millionaires of some manufacturers, have you added one dollar to the wealth of the country ? Is the country at the end of a period of 50 or 100 years in any better position of self defence, in any better position to maintain its industries against the aggression of outside nations, than it was at the beginning of that period ? Take away the bonus at the end of 50 years, take away the bonus at the end of 100 years and you are just where you were at the time that you began, with this difference, that the people are just so many millions worse off than they were at the beginning of that period.
I am not going to enter into the large question of protection at this time, but I want to make it perfectly clear the aim of this bounty, treating it in the abstract; and having regard too to the actual facts of the case. I would be very sorry to have it understood by the great agricultural classes of this country, I was in favour of bounties in any shape or form. I am not in favour of them, because I recognize that the system is unfair to the great agricultural class of this country. I recognize, as I say, the importance of the great iron and steel industry. But I recognize as of still more importance that the manufacturers should understand from 250
whom their bread and butter is to come. I want these manufacturers to understand that they cannot play fast and loose with the Conservative party. I want them to recollect that it is the Conservative party to whom they are indebted for the measure of prosperity they are enjoying in this country to-day. I do not think that in the past they have shown that gratitude they should have shown. Be that as it may, I believe that the way to bring about a remedy for the state of things we have at the present time, the way to bring about an adequate system of protection in this country, which I believe is all important to our continued prosperity, is to let the manufacturers and merchants, and agriculturists all understand that there will be no special preference given to any one ; that we are going to mete out equal justice to all ; that we are going to recognize that no one industry Stands by itself, and that whenever one industry has to be kept up at the permanent expense of another. there is something wrong. The great principle enunciated by the Conservative party in the past and by the Conservative party of the present, is that all industries shall work together, each one assisting the other ; and that in this way, the only safe position we can take, the only safe position any man can take who believes that a protective system, reasonably high, is necessary in this country, is to say : You gentlemen want special favours, and although we would be glad to assist you, we cannot assist you unless you join with us in developing one great system upon general lines that will be fair to all the industries of the coup-try.	.

I would like to ask the Minister of Finance a question. This resolution which says, ' from steel produced in Canada from ingredients of which not less than fifty per cent of the weight thereof consists of pig-iron made in Canada '-what kind of ore must that.be, Canadian ore or American ore ?
That is in the manufacture of steel ?
Yes.

While the question of ore enters into the manufacture of pig-iron, after the pig-iron is made in Canada there is no question of the ore as respects the bounty on steel. The question of native or foreign ore arises entirely as respects the manufacture of pig-iron.

But as the bounty is paid in respect of productions made from the steel, I think you should prefer the pig-iron that is made entirely from Canadian ore. That opens up this question :	You may
have smelters in Canada using Canadian ore and you may have them using American ore. Now if they use Canadian ore, that gives work for Canadian vessels in carrying that



ore from Michipicoten-which is practically the only point in Canada where we have iron at present on the great lakes ; but, if you use American ore, that gives work to American vessels. In a concern where they produce both steel and iron as well, they would decidedly prefer to use Canadian ore if the preference was given to steel manufactured from Canadian ore by way of bounty.

If they use foreign ore they suffer for it, if I may so speak, by reason of the lesser bounty they would get on pig-iron. It is at that stage of the process that the distinction is made. They will not get the same bounty on that pig-iron as they would if it were made from native ore.

But if this bounty was paid only on pig-iron that was made exclusively of Canadian ore, that would1 give a great impetus I contend to Canadian ore. It would result in the employment in Canada of a great many men in mining ore and as I before pointed .out it would result in giving employment to Canadian vessels. The fact of the matter is that at the present time the Canadian shipping trade is greatly hampered owing to the fact that it cannot engage in the American ore trade which is one of the biggest interests that the American vessels have. The grain trade being at an end the American vessels can go into the ore carrying trade, carrying the ore from different points on the American side to points on Lake Erie. Canadian vessels, by reason of the coasting laws, are estopped from participating in that trade and they can only have recourse in a limited way to the ore trade in carrying ore from Michipicoten to Midland or from Michipicoten to Hamilton. I think this clause should be limited to pig-iron manufactured entirely from Canadian ore.

That would be an entire departure from the principle which has governed these steel bounties from the beginning. The only distinction we have made between imported and native ore is in regard to the manufacture of pig-iron and not in regard to the manufacture of steel, and that has been done from the beginning.

Whether it was right or wrong at the beginning I submit that this measure should be framed in such a way as to foster Canadian trade. If the bounties were made payable only on steel manufactured from Canadian pig-iron it will be to the interest of the manufacturer to use Canadian ores exclusively, but if a free market is given to American ore the result is very different. I grant that this may appeal strongly to the interests of the Sydney concern because the ore used there is known as foreign ore.
It is from Newfoundland.

That is classed, I assume, as foreign ore. In that case we are discriminating practically against the balance of the Dominion or against the iron industries that are operating in other parts of the Dominion and against the ores of the upper lakes.

I find in the Act of 1894 that the bounty is confined entirely to pig-iron manufactured from Canadian ore. Then in 1897 I find that the bounty is given to pig-iron manufactured from 50 per cent of Canadian ore. What led the government to make this discrimination ?
My impression is that the distinction between native and foreign ore was made earlier than that. Possibly my hon. friend (Mr. Gour-ley) may be correct.
I have looked at the Acts this evening.

If my hon. friend has looked at the Acts I am quite content to accept his statement. I remember at the time the bounties were dealt with that the only point of difference was that some hon. gentlemen thought that we should class Newfoundland ore as Canadian and treat it as our own ore.
Has the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) a case in his mind to illustrate the point ?

Yes, in Midland and also in Hamilton where they have smelters they use large quantities of the now celebrated Michipicoten ore which is brought from Lake Superior. Under this resolution it is immaterial whether the ore comes from Michipicoten or from Two Harbours or from any point on the American side.
No, there is no distinction as regards pig-iron.

Certainly, but once done with pig-iron we come to the question of steel and the point is! this : The bounty is payable in respect of steel produced from pig-iron. If that pig-iron is altogether made of Canadian ores you will give Canadian ores the advantage, but, on the other hand, if the pig-iron is made from American ore you are giving the American ore to that extent an advantage, because, I think I am correct in saying that the American ore is brought in free of duty. I say, in the first place, that if you were to state in your resolution that all pig-iron that enters into the constitution or make-up of steel must be made of Canadian ore, you are giving a premium on Canadian pig-iron, and you are going to encourage the mining of ore at Michipicoten! and the development of other Canadian mines on the shore of Lake Superior which can be developed. By this resolution you are giving the Americans the benefit of our bounty system, and we are

now in this position on the upper lakes that Canadian bottoms can get very little to do. The grain season being at an end they are not allowed to participate in the American coasting trade by carrying ore, and the result is that Canadian vessels are to-day practically carrying for nothing to meet expenses. It is a well known fact that to-day Canadian bottoms are carrying grain from Fort William to Montreal at four cents a bushel, a rate which at one time was looked upon as being simply ridiculous. There are one or two courses open to them- either to tie these vessels up at the dock or to carry at these ruinous rates as they regard them. If we had these bounties on pig-iron produced from the ore found on the shores of Lake Superior we should develop the production of ore there as much as possible. Canadian vessels are not alone in carrying of this ore from Michipicoten to United States ports, for the reason that it is not a contravention of the coasting laws, but American vessels may indulge in that trade. In the first place you hamper Canadian bottoms by leaving this wide open to American as well as Canadian ore, and in the next place you prevent a larger user of Canadian ore by not providing that the pig-iron going into the steel to which the bounty applies shall be exclusively Canadian. I think that is a question that the minister might fairly consider and see if this cannot be done.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett), if he wants to present that view, ought to deal with the manufacture of pig iron and not with steel ; whatever force there is in his argument is against the use of imported ore for making pig-iron.

I admit that we get the benefit of the manufacture of pig-iron, but I say we should go a step further and provide that the steel that is to earn this bounty shall be the product exclusively of Canadian ore and in that way you would increase the user of Canadian ore and give employment to Canadian vessels.

In so far as the use of Canadian products are required at all this requirement applies to Canadian pig-iron. The iron is made in Canada with Canadian labour at Canadian furnaces, and no matter what the source of the ore is it then becomes Canadian product. When you come to the next process, to the manufacture of steel, the pig-iron made in Canada, in Canadian furnaces and with Canadian labour, becomes to all intents and purposes a Canadian product, and must be so treated in the next stage. The argument of my hon. friend seems to be that in the manufacture of pig-iron we should either forbid the use of imported ore or make a larger discrimination than we are making.

Let me illustrate the point. At Collingwood I think at a verv 2501
early date a steel concern is to be under way. Assuming that they wish to earn this bounty and assuming that the law should say that they should only use pig-iron which was composed exclusively of Canadian ores to entitle them to the bounty on steel and that if they use in the manufacture of that steel product any American ore, they would be estopped from earning any portion of the bounty, that ore would go either to the smelter at Midland or to the smelter at Hamilton, and they would say : We cannot earn the bounty on steel unless we use exclusively Canadian produced pig-iron ; in other words pig-iron made from Canadian' ores, the result would be that they would only buy pig-iron made from Canadian ore, but if it is left open as it is, it is immaterial to these producers of steel whether they buy pig-iron made of American ore or Canadian ore.
If it were necessary to mix it in order to make steel.

That opens up another field, and if there is to be a blending of ores then the bounty should be paid in respect to the Canadian ore only and not the American ore. But it might be possible to produce the steel from iron that was made exclusively from Canadian ore.
They are not doing it.
That is on account of the uses they put it to.

I wish to ask the minister a question with reference to the amount of duty all told that would be paid on -wire rods three-eighths of an inch in diameter. I understand that we did pay $3 bounty for the production of the iron, and $3 more for the production of the steel. Will these rods be made from this steel which has already received a bounty of practically $6 a ton? If so, the entire 'bounty on these wire rods would be $12.

My hon. friend's calculation is quite correct except with regard to the first process. He has taken the bounty on the pig-iron at $3, but of course if it were made from imported ore it would be only $2. Subject to that correction, my hon. friend is substantially correct. Of course, the persons who produce these things are not the same in all cases.	*
If this is intended to give a preference to the Canadian ore entering into the production of pig-iron, why should' it not be equally so in regard to the steel \

There is some point in the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett), but it is so radical a departure from the conditions in the past,

that if we adopted such a policy it might have a very serious effect on some of the furnaces. I am inclined to think that, the Ontario furnaces would not use entirely Canadian ore, and we know that two of the large concerns in Nova Scotia depend wholly upon Newfoundland ore, and to say that they should be'shut out entirely from the bounty on steel because they imported Newfoundland ore would be a serious proposition. Although my hou. friend may think there is some reason.for it, yet the effect of it would be to close them up.

Conceding for the sake of argument that there must of necessity be a blending of American ore with Canadian ore to produce pig-iron, that would make steel, then there should be a higher bounty paid on the Canadian ore than on the American ore. The proportion of the bounty should be higher on the Canadian ore going into the manufacture than upon the American or foreign ore.

What would be the effect of the, application of that principle if we were to apply it to the coal that is used in the production of this iron? It is found in Cape Breton that they must import some portion of their raw material from Newfoundland, and they have gone as far as Spain and Norway for it. In the western part of Canada they get the iron ore from the Lake Superior region, but they get their coal from the United States. If you apply the principle that because a portion of the ore in eastern Canada is imported it should not be entitled to this concession, then it might be said that the iron masters in western Canada are not entitled to the concession because they import American coal for the purpose of manufacturing. I fancy that the object we have in view is to develop the manufacture of iron ore in Canada, and, the place whence the ore comes is a matter of comparative unimportance, because the cost of the ore is a very small factor in the cost of production. Besides, we are not in possession of the expert evidence that was presented when this particular kind of legislation was first introduced into this House. The policy was adopted after most mature consideration, and after consultation with men who thoroughly understood the fluxing and manufacture of ores. I would look with considerable doubt upon any attempt to change a plan that was adopted after most mature consideration.

I think that possibly the discussion to-night has taken a much wider range than was expected by the Minister of Finance when he moved this resolution. No doubt, that is an indication of the general interest felt to-day in the wider question of protection. It would appear to me that the manner in which on every occasion when the opportunity arises, the discussion, beginning no matter where it may, always
