Medical men as a rule hold that specifics should be avoided as much as possible, and that general treatment is preferable.
Some very good citizens sell them.
And recommend them.

It is better to avoid their use, however, and therefore I believe that in this case the action of the government would be more satisfactory to the company

and to the country generally if they avoided what they describe themselves as specific treatment and resorted to good general practice. To my mind the hon. Minister of Customs has made a most complete and sudden volte-face. He turned a summersault of a most extraordinary character when, in justifying the course of the government in coming to the rescue of this particular industry and resorting to a specific treatment for the cure of a specific ailment, he declared, without a shadow of evidence, that so far as a great many other industries are concerned, which are complaining, their position was due to no fault on thetpart of the government or tariff, but entirely to their own lack of good management. Why did he not apply that rule to the specific case with which we are dealing ? In this case he did not attribute any fault to the management, so that we may conclude that if other industries could make out an equally strong case, the government would not press against them this charge of mismanagement or lack of ability, but would provide a specific remedy to meet each specific case. The result would be that this government would stand prepared, in every case in which this tariff is proved ineffective, to come to the rescue of the particular industry in distress. If so, I would like to know how much further this government has to go in order to establish itself fully in the position of being in favour of protection to Canadian industry and the development to the utmost possible extent of such industries-in fact of going to the utmost length to which the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is prepared to go in doing everything possible in order that Canadians may supply exclusively the manufactured products we require.
But this is a new industry in the country. These articles are not yet introduced in the country.

These particular articles that are now being introduced-but how does that help the hon. gentleman ? If he is prepared, in order to introduce into a manufacturing industry of this country, some new articles, to come to the assistance of that industry, is he not a protectionist up to the hilt V

I only mention that because the hon. gentleman was saying that other industries in existence, which were suffering, might as well come forward and be similarly dealt with. 1 point out that this is not a manufactory of certain goods, which .has been in existence for years and is suffering, but it is an industry which is bringing into existence a new line of manufactured product.

This industry is simply producing a particular form of article which has not hitherto been made in this country, Mr. BELL.
but it is not a new industry. If the hon. gentleman were to make in his establishment a new kind of biscuit or confectionary, he might just as well claim that he was establishing a new industry. This steel company is turning out steel billets, but these particular billets, to which this exceptional protection is to be given, are simply to be rolled to a rather smaller size, or, in the case of plates, they are rolled to a greater width and are a little more weighty. It is not a new industry we are assisting, but only varied products of an industry already established. Therefore, I think the hon. gentleman has been rather unfortunate in his interruption.
Does it. not bring into this country an entirely new class of machinery, which is not in existence at present V
No, it does not.
Yes, it does.	.

It simply means that whereas the company have been rolling their steel to a size of four inches square, they are about to take that four inch square billet and reduce it to a size of three-quarter inch round. That is all it means. And, instead of the billets being four inches square, they are to be passed through smaller rollers until they are reduced" to a diameter of three-quarters of an inch. They have been producing iron of that size at New Glasgow. They have not been producing wire rods, and the only difference between the rod and the steel billet is that the rod is rolled a little longer to a smaller diameter. To pretend that it is a new product, one might as well say that a new pattern of calico produced in a cotton mill is a new product. It is merely a slight change from what the manufacturer has been making all the time. But the great point is this. AYhy does the government hesitate ? Is it possible that the government hopes to deceive that great class of voters, the consumers, to whom they played during eighteen years of opposition V Is it possible that by refusing to change their tariff but effecting exactly the same purpose by means of a bounty they hope to delude the people into the belief that this government, so ready to go to the assistance of a suffering industry, is really a free trade government. To my mind it is impossible to find any other reason for their action in this matter. And while I am glad indeed, for the sake of an industry in my own province, which is of the very highest importance, and which both sides of this House will admit is one of the fundamental industries of any country that is going to develop manufacturing ascendency, that the government has adopted this course, but I would be much better pleased if it would do it in such a frank fashion as would rank it in the safe,

strong, defensible position of being openly and avowedly prepared to assist tlie industries of Canada, and enable Canada to develop from a mere producer of raw materials into a centre of varied manufacturing industries embracing every achievement in that direction possible to our natural resources and people. The criticism of the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) condemning the government because it is treating this iron and steel industry in a friendly manner, and describing it as an industry which is not legitimate to Canada., is most amazing. In what country could the iron industry be more legitimate than Canada Y We have every one of the raw materials which enter into the production of iron. We have a suitable climate, a people unexcelled in their adaptability to all industrial processes, and a climate that is favourable to severe labour. In fact we have an ideal country in which to produce iron. We are alongside a country which is leading in iron trade in the world, and' has yet no greater facilities for that trade than we have. There is this one difference between the United States and Canada, and that is that in the one case, undiscouraged by the failures that attend its earliest years, the government of the United States went from one stage of protection to another, and by showing itself in favour of protection and pressing that remedy home to the last requirements of the industry, succeeded in establishing it in the unrivalled position in which it is to-day. There is no other difference between the two countries.
And there can be no question that if we stand as loyally, firmly and believingly at the back of the iron industry of this country as they did in the United States, we may hope at an early day to see Canada become what, so far as natural resources are concerned, she is calculated to become, one of the great iron producing countries in the world. No doubt, at the back of that, progress, will follow exactly what is being hoped for by the government in this matter. Here the government is helping not only the production of raw material, but also-a distinction properly drawn by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver)-the second industry of producing wire and nails from that iron. The government is not only offering assistance to the great company producing foundation article, the iron, but is also seeking to add another industry to the working outfit of this country, employing labour, adding new centres of population, increasing the home market for the farmers, adding to the imports, swelling the trade of this country. By this action unquestionably, if they stand loyally at the back of this industry and do it frankly as protectionists, they will add one industry to another until they will have added enormously to the productive powers and population of Canada, and we will have wiped out what, to my mind, is a reproach
to Canada that, in an article which she could produce, she is dependent upon the United States. The government has entered upon a good work; let them go forward in that work. And I would suggest that it would be better, in the interest of the manufacturers, in the interest of the country, and better in order to establish that confidence which will attract foreign capital to come freely into this country and bring the necessary population with it. that the government should enter upon this course in such a fashion as shall convince all that their action is not merely temporary, not a mere specific for a special case of illness, but a carefully thought out policy which it is not only prepared to apply for the moment, but to guarantee interested parties in this country or out of it that it is ready and determined to continue as long it remains in power as a government.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the first time that you have had the painful experience of seeing the Finance Minister standing face to face with the consequence of his own blunders. Nor is it the first time we have seen the Finance Minister asking the authority of parliament to pass the hat to recoup by bounties industries that have been injured by his policy. The Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), whom I see smiling as he always does, challenged this side of the House to point out an industry in Canada that was not prosperous. Any hon. gentleman might make that challenge. But let me remind him that, if our industries generally are prosperous, it is because he and his friends had not the courage to take away the protection that has been given to those industries by a previous government. But there are some exceptions to our prosperity, and those exceptions can be traced in every instance to the removal of protection by this government. I challenge the hon. gentleman to controvert that statement. I say that there is not an industry in which they have taken away substantial protection which is not suffering materially, or which is not coming here and asking for protection. But instead of giving the protection which his policy has taken away, he is asking the people to put their hands in their pockets and recoup those industries by bounties. The hon. gentleman said we must have protection or bounties. I would ask him how he would like to have protection taken away from the business that he has made a great success, partly by his ability as a business man and partly by the protection given to that industry, and an allowance of bounties made that would assist him temporarily and for the renewal of which he would be obliged to come and ask from time to time. If he would not consent to that, how can he approve of the proposition made by the Finance Minister to-day? The hon. gentleman tried to

draw a fine distinction based upon tlie idea that this is a new industry. But the government are giving bounties not merely to the new industries that are mentioned, but also to production of iron, which is an old industry in this country. There is absolutely no difference for practical purposes whether it is an industry which is being expanded and extended or a new industry that is to be built up. The hon. gentleman recognizes that, for he proposes to treat them alike. I do not know anything more at variance with the hon. gentleman's own experience as a business man than the policy of bounties. I do not know anything more at variance with the experience of every practical man. Of course, we make some allowance for hon. gentlemen brought up in what I may, without offence, call the narrow school. None doubt the sincerity of the Finance Minister. But many doubt his theories. The industries of the country have good reason to doubt his theories. He was brought up in a school whose chief idea was to worry and harass every industry in the country, to look with distorted eye, almost with a bloodshot eye, on every industry that received a particle of protection. Now, however, he finds himself face to face with the great responsibilities of the high position of Minister of Finance. He must deal with great practical questions. But he never moves from conviction, nor will he unbend any of the things he has learned. He moves under pressure. He still thinks that every particle of protection is an evil. The only thing that causes him to recede from his position is the strong pressure of the business interests of the country, whose dissatisfaction, he fears, will cost him some votes. Now, what would be an ideal man for Minister of Finance? If I were selecting a Minister of Finance, I should not select one different physically or intellectually from the one we have. But I would select one who would unlearn everything the hon. gentleman has learned. I would select one who would1 act from conviction, and who would be moved by the broad spirit of protection that pervades this country. That it does pervade the country we can see by the attitude of the hon. gentleman's own followers. We had, for instance, the example of wabbling of the hon. gentleman from Alberta (Mr. Oliver). He found fault with everything and condemned everything, yet he was able to support the government. He told us that we must have cheap iron. The government some time ago took the duties off iron, one of the great errors they are trying to repair. And I would ask the hon. member for Alberta to point out a single instance where we have had cheaper goods as a result of the lowering of duty. I- challenge the hon. gentleman to say that there has been a single article purchased cheaper by reason of the government having lowered Mr. CLANCY.
the duties on iron. But the government have considerably crippled this industry. And what does the Finance Minister think will happen at the end of four years when these bounties shall cease ? The hon. gentleman will have to mend his ways between now and then, if he is still Finance Minister. But if he does not mend his ways and the people will still be deceived, >what will be the position of these industries? They must come back, every one of them, and ask for additional bounties. They cannot maintain themselves. They have lost their own market, and as a compensation we have to give them bounties instead of giving them protection, which would result, in a large measure, in supporting them at the expense of the foreigner. Now, what is the position of the workingman in this country ? Under a proper system of protection he has a day's work, whereas under the present system it means that he is deprived of that day's work because he has lost the field, and he must put his hand into his pocket and contribute something to help his neighbour.
Now, I do not propose to offer any opposition to this measure, because I think it is necessary under the circumstances. At the same time, I do not think it is a wise policy, I think it an extremely unwise policy. It is merely a policy of shifting, merely a policy of expediency ; an hon. friend near me says it is wabbling. It is not even respectable wabbling. However, I welcome anything that will for the time being give relief to this industry that the hon. gentlemen have in a sense destroyed. They have come down and have to some extent repaired the harm they had done, but at the expense of the taxpayers of this country. They did the same thing with respect to the binder twine industry. The duty was taken off the binder twine altogether, and after the hon. gentlemen had ruined that industry practically, they passed the hat around to help the manufacturers of binder twine. They are now passing the hat around again to help the iron industry. But this bounty system will not give them the home market. The American producer will still come in and sell alongside of them, as he does in respect to the binder twine industry. It is simply taxing our own people for the support of these industries instead of taxing the foreign manufacturer. It is about time, it seems to me, that we should shift the burden. I have only to repeat what I said at the outset, that I do not know of any more unwelcome spectacle than to see ministers sitting on that side of the House who came in seven years ago with a great flourish of trumpets, promising to reform the tariff, and they have not made a single reform. I challenge them now to point to a single substantial reform, a single change they have made in the tariff to compensate those from whom they took away protection. I am going to support the boun-

ty, not because I believe it is a wise principle, but because I tbink it is necessary to do something to keep this iron and steel industry on its feet.

I understand that these bounties are given in order to stimulate the industry of iron and steel, I do not understand that they are given for protection. I understand that the people who started this industry are not able to purchase the machinery and to carry it on successfully without some assistance from the country. In other words, this bounty is given as an encouragement to them in their work. Now, it seems to me that unless we have the raw material in our country, unless we have sufficient iron and coal in proximity, it is only a waste of money to give bounties to stimulate that industry. After you have encouraged this steel and iron industry by a bounty, after you have got it to work and it is then still unable to stand up on its own merits permanently, what is the use of giving the bounty ? As I say, in order that the industry may be permanently successful it must have the raw material, the coal and iron in proximity to each other. If you have to import the raw material you cannot be successful. I heard thejion. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) complaining that they are paying duties on iron made from ore brought from the United States. Now, if you are going to bring ore from the United States and coal from the United States, you had better let the United States manufacture the iron, because you are only throwing away your money by giving it bounties.
An lion. MEMBER. What about the cotton industry in England ?

They can get the raw material cheaper than any other country because they have got the shipping to bring it in cheaper than any other country ; that is why the cotton industry succeeds in England. The iron industry succeeds there because they have both the coal and the iron. But it is no use for us under any circumstances to try to bolster up manufacturers of raw material of which we do not possess within our own borders. I heard the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) say a few minutes ago that they had the grandest country under heaven for the manufacture of iron. If they have, then they must lack men of enterprise and intelligence to carry on the industry. If you have got the raw material and if you have got the right kind of men, you do not need any protection. I do not like the bonusing system, either in this or in any other industry. If you have got the right kind of men with any snap about them, they ought to make the industry a success without the assistance of bounties. Still, in this case, if these men are suffering, if they feel obliged to give up the enterprise and to take their money out of the country unless we help to
set them on their feet, I am willing to help them, but all the same I say it is a wrong principle.

I want to ask the Finance Minister a few questions. I would like to know how much of the ore that is manufactured or smelted in Deseronto is imported into this country. They make a different kind of iron to what is made in Nova Scotia, it is called charcoal iron. I would like to know how much ore they imported. I would like to know whether the increased amount of bounties you are proposing to give will be sufficient to tide the companies that are supposed to be in financial difficulty over the trouble they haVe got into. I think the Finance Minister ought to give us some information with respect to the reasons why he brought this up at so late a date. I have no doubt he has had interviews with the company, discussion and correspondence, and I think the House is entitled to that information. I presume it is not necessary to say anything with reference to the position of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, the Finance Minister is perfectly familiar with it. It is said they are in the best place in the world to manufacture iron. The town of Sydney gave the company 500 acres of land fronting on the harbour. The bounties they expected to receive would be sufficient to pay for the plant and to set them going in a successful manner. Now, if these things are true, if Cape Breton is the best place in the world to manufacture iron, there must have been great mismanagement in this matter. If there has been mismanagement in it why should the people be taxed to make right the mistakes that have been made by a particular company ? I differ entirely from my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), I am not in favour of bounties.
Neither am I.
You may not be in favour of them, but you are going to support them, and it looks as if you were in favour of them.

I did not say whether I was in favour of bounties or not. I say that on general principles I am opposed to bounties, but if lion.' gentlemen opposite have destroyed industries by taking away their protection, I am willing to give bounties or anything else to help them out.

The hon. gentleman only does it as the 'best thing possible, and not because he likes it. He is in favour of a fair measure of protection which I think is by far the better policy. I see that the president of the Consolidated Lake Superior Company has issued a circular letter which appeared in the Toronto ' Mail and Empire ' of the 28th July, in which he says that unless the stockholders of the company take up the bonds amounting to 812,500,000 the

property 'will fall into the hands of the creditors. That seems to me to be a very strange condition of affairs. I would like the hon. Minister of Finance to tell us whe-there these bounties are going to be sufficient to tide these people over their difficulties. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company last year, according to the answer given by the hon. Minister of Finance, to a question asked in this House, received bounties to the amount of $885,903, and the total bounties paid last year on iron and steel were $1,245,382. It does seem to me that if we cannot manufacture iron and steel under such bounties as these it is folly for us to increase them, and if it is because of the bad management of these companies that they have had such poor success then I think they ought to be allowed to go to the wall and let other men take hold of the business who would be able to conduct it in a more successful way.

I think the first question my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) asked was in reference to the operation of a charcoal iron furnace at Deser-onto. I understand the ore is imported almost wholly from the United States.
What bounty do they get per ton ?

Two dollars per ton on the imported ore and on any portion they make from native or6 they, of course, get a higher bounty. In regard to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, I have had frequent communications with representatives of that company. I am not authorized to say that they will regard this as entirely satisfactory. I think it will enable them to continue their operations at present, and that they will regaM this as meeting their difficulties for the time being.
What proportion of the enterprise is in operation now ?

I have not had any very recent communication with them, but I have seen what appeared in the press. I understand that the other day they stopped a portion of the work, and I saw by a subsequent telegram that it was stated that they had resumed it, but I have no information upon that point other than what I saw in the public press. In regard to the operations at Sault Ste. Marie, there have been no representations made to us lately on this subject. The condition of the industry was presented to us at the beginning of the session, and a proposal was made in regard to steel rails, and the arrangement then announced respecting duty on rails was based on representations so made, although, of course, it applies as well to any other mill in Canada which may make steel rails. As far as I am aware, the mill at Sault Ste. Marie is the only Mr. WILSON.
mill which intends to make steel rails. I have had no communication from them lately, and I am not in a position to give any further information upon that point.
Have they carried out their contract for the supply of steel rails ?

No, they failed to carry out their contract for the supply of steel rails during the time specified. They did supply a quantity later oil, but they did not supply the quantity that the contract mentioned. They, however, supplied a smaller quantity. I am not able to say anything as to their future operations.
Resolution reported, read the first and second times, and agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 238) respecting bounties bn iron and steel.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton), moved the second reading of Bill (No. 232) to amend the Manitoba Grain Act, 1900.
Would the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Clifford Sit-ton) make some statement as to the Bill before.it is read a second time ?

When introducing this Bill I made a general statement in regard to its purport, and I think perhaps a detailed explanation would be more intelligible in taking the clauses up in committee. I may say in a general way that the Bill is a result of the experience of the last year or two in connection with the difficulties of handling grain in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. There has been a 'great deal of difficulty in connection with the transportation question for some years, and a condition under which practically the men who were in the elevator and warehouse business were enabled to compel the producers of grain to sell their grain to them directly, because of the fact that they were unable to procure cars for shipment themselves. An amendment was introduced a year ago, chapter 19 of the statutes of 1902, which was designed to meet that condition of affairs by permitting farmers to ship directly, giving them power to order their cars directly, and compelling railway companies to furnish. cars directly to them. In addition to that a number of other changes were made concerning the regulation of the shipping business as originally provided in the Manitoba Grain Act, 1900. The Act of 1902 was largely experimental and it was known to be experimental at the time, because it was known that it would bring

about considerable changes in the shipping of grain, and it was not known until actual experience had demonstrated how the provisions of the law would work.
I may say that the provisions of the law of 1902 have given great satisfaction to the farmers of Manitoba and the North-west Territories. I do not mean that the Act has been regarded by the farmers as being perfect by any means, but it has' been regarded as being a vast improvement upon the legislation as it stood upon the statute-book-before. The privilege which this Act gave to the farmers of ordering their cars directly and shipping directly is considered by them to be an extremely valuable privilege. The grain-growers of Manitoba and the North-west have formed an association and they have discussed this question of the shipment of grain at great length, and at the different meetings which they have held the representatives of the railway companies have been invited to meet them and the subject has been discussed very fully. During the present session of parliament the grain-growers sent a deputation to Ottawa and the grain-dealers of Manitoba and the North-west Territories also sent a deputation and they met here and fully discussed the proposed changes in the law. A short time ago they submitted to me a Bill which was practically the result of their deliberations and was in the nature of an arrangement which was agreed to by all parties. The railway companies have also been consulted in regard to the provisions of the Bill, and while the Bill does not absolutely meet the views of any of the conflicting interests, yet I am satisfied from the information at our disposal that it may be regarded as a satisfactory measure. The principal provisions of the Bill are :	In section 3
to provide for the appointment of deputy warehouse commissioners. The original Act provided for the appointment of a warehouse commissioner and it has been found that owing to the duties that have devolved upon him and the enormous increase of the business of shipping grain due to the increased production, he has been unable to find sufficient time for the discharge of all his duties. It is certain that we shall require to appoint one or more deputy commissioners under this clause. The effect of the 4th section is to bring track buyers of grain under the provisions of the law which require licenses to be taken out by persons dealing in grain. The 5th section provides by an amendment to section 10 that the weighmasters and their! assistants, in addition to the other information which they are required to report, shall report as to whether or not the cars which they examine are in bad order. Section 6 deals with the making of returns by the warehouse men owning or operating terminal elevators as required by section 24 of the Act. Section 7 gives the commissioner power to deal with disputes in regard to applications for sites for
elevators and warehouses. The effect of section 8 is to require persons operating country elevators or country warehouses to receive as a matter of duty under the law the first six standard grades of wheat established and described in the general Inspection Act. Section 9 makes provision to exempt the elevator owner from receiving grain when he has not sufficient accommodation for that purpose. Section 10 makes provision which deals with the duty of the elevator man in regard to the shipments of grain when the owner desires it shall be shipped. The provision in the existing law was found to create a difficulty by reason of the fact that when a person who owned an elevator was unable to secure shipping facilities he was still compelled to keep the grain without making any charge for it. Section 11 provides for the amendment to section 34 of the original Act by adding a subsection the effect of which I will explain when we reach the committee stage. The effect of section 12 is to make an amendment to section 35 which provides for the giving of notice in case that grain goes out of condition in the elevator. Section 13 makes a change in section 39, the effect of which can only be shown by comparison and there are some verbal changes which I shall explain in the committee. Section 14 makes provision for the erection of flat warehouses which is substantially the same as in the Act of 1902, but the section is required because the repeal of the Act of 1902 does not bring into effect legislation which was repealed by that Act itself, so that we have to re-enact. Section 15 is new and it is simply to prevent a person getting a warehouse site from the railway company and allowing it to stand	without proceeding	with the
work. Section 16 provides in detail for the construction of loading platforms. Section 17 deals with the duties of grain commission merchants. When they sell on commission, they are required to in a certain specified time report the quantity sold and render a statement to the consignor. One section deals with the necessity of their taking out a license. Section 18 is the same as the section dealing with the same subject in the Act of 1902. Section 19 amends section 50 of the original Act, and requires the chief inspector, in addition to making a report to the railway officials, to make a return to the commissioner. Section 20 deals with penalties. Section 21 makes provision with reference to the distribution of cars. This is the most important feature of the Act. Section 61 is new. It provides that the provisions of the Act shall not apply to grain which is shipped westward of the British Columbia boundary. It was found in actual practice that the result of the Act making provision respecting the distribution of cars was to prevent the railway companies, on shipping on British Columbia orders or on orders for the

orient, to supply the cars, because the law would not permit them to do so except in a certain way; and it has been agreed by all concerned that the Act shall be amended] so that it shall not apply to the shipment of grain when it is consigned to any point west of the boundary line between British Columbia and the North-west Territories. The Bill as drawn says the Pacific coast, but I propose to have that amended by changing it to the boundary line of British Columbia. Section 62 deals with the licensing of track buyers. Sections 22 and 23 amend the forms of storage receipts in the schedule in compliance with the amendments to the Act in other places.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

Will the minister make a short statement as to the actual condition of affairs in the North-west to-day-whether the car famine has been largely overcome, whether there has been an increase of elevators, and whether generally the grievances which formerly existed in connection with this matter have been ameliorated to any extent.

My information is that at the present time there is no difficulty in regard to the shipment of grain, because practically the whole of last year's crop is shipped out. The difficulty as to car shortage will of course not arise again until the new wheat comes in, and what we are trying to do in this legislation is to provide a- satisfactory method for the distribution of cars. This legislation will not provide any more cars or increase the quantity of rolling stock, but I think it will result in a far more satisfactory distribution of cars.
Do the railway companies show a disposition to provide an increased number of cars for the trade V Has the situation been improved in that respect V

Yes. My information is that the railway companies have shown a disposition to put on all the rolling stock they could get. That question was gone into very fully during the early part of last winter, at the time the car shortage was very acute, and I think everybody who had anything to do with the railway companies was satisfied that they were doing their best, although they were seriously to blame for not forseeing what was to come, and making adequate provision for it. Since that time they have been making every effort to provide adequate rolling stock and prevent a shortage in the future. Whether they will have sufficient [DOT]cars to move the next crop it is difficult to say at present. That depends to some extent on the deliveries to the cars and to , Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
some extent on Providence as to the amount of wheat there will be to be shipped out. No one can form any very definite idea as to that until practically the last week of the harvest. My observation in Manitoba and the North-west Territories is that people have very little idea of how much wheat they are going to have until a few days before the wheat is ready to be cut. The climatic condition of the last two weeks practically decides whether the crop will be a phenomenal one or an average one. The present indications are that in the North-west Territories it will be very good, in some parts of Manitoba it will be very good, and in other parts somewhat light. On the whole it is not to be expected that it well be as large as the crops of the last three years.
Has there been any improvement in regard to elevators and storehouses V

There has been an enormous increase in the amount of elevator accommodation. Elevators are being constructed rapidly all over the country, andi the accommodation will be vastly greater than it was last year.

I might point out also that a good deal of the trouble during the last two years was due to the increased acreage sown. Many of the farmers had no granaries, and as soon as they threshed their wheat they were anxious to put it in cars or in an elevator. In other words, they wished the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to furnish them with granary and warehouse accommodation at a moment's notice. That will of course largely improve itself as time goes on. Not only have a great many elevators been built by the grain companies at the railway stations, and the railway companies have increased their elevator accommodation, but many farmers have built granaries. At the present time the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Montreal Transportation Company report that they are carrying cargoes westward, and are coming east light, because all the grain is out.
On section 3,
Is it the intention to have those commissioners located at AVinnipeg or to place them at other imints throughout the province ?

They will have to be located at outlying points. The difficulty which arises with the commissioner at AVinnipeg is that he is liable to get demands from different parts of the country at the same time, which necessitate a very large amount of travel and delay. They will have to be located at points whence they can get readily to places where complaints arise. The commissioner at AVinnipeg will have general supervision over their duties.

On section 9,
Wouid the hon. minister please explain this section ?

The law as it stood made some provision requiring the elevator men to take in wheat whenever it was offered. They claimed that they were liable-they were advised that they were liable-if they did not take the grain when it was offered, even if their elevators were full and they could not get cars to ship. This provides that they shall not he required to take the grain in when they have not room for it.
On section 10,

As I read this clause, only the farmer who has a full car load of grain can take advantage of this provision of the Act. Now, there are a great many people living at a distance from the railway who are entirely left out of the benefits of this clause. A man living within ten or twelve miles of a railway station can call for a car and load it. But the man living at a distance must use the elevator. Now, there are many new settlers coming into this country who have not 1,000 or 1,500 bushels of wheat to ship the first year. But if two or three farmers together have enough wheat of a certain grade in the elevator to make up a carload, why' should they not be allowed to combine and order a car ? If this is not allowed, the elevator people, knowing that these small growers cannot get cars, will have them completely at their mercy, and will buy their wheat at what they choose to give for it.

I suppose that what my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) means is that if say three farmers, none of whom have enough grain to make a carload, could, by combining their warehouse receipts, make up a carload, they should be allowed to order a car to take the grain out.

That is exactly what I mean.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, I may explain that, as the matter stood under the Act of 1902, we had given the farmer the privilege of ordering a ear to a loading platform or into the yard. But we did not give him the privilege of ordering a car to the elevator, even though he had his grain there. This is to cover that defect, and to enable a farmer who has his grain stored to order a car to the elevator and ship it himself and sell it direct. I do not know that there would be any objection to the amendment suggested by my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), but I would like to hear what the other members from Manitoba and the North-west Territories have to say about it before it is agreed to.

I would remind the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) that the parties to whom he refers are still able to combine, as many did during last season, and fill their car at a loading platform. But, as the hon. minister has stated, the defect of the Bill last year was that no farmer could compel the railway company to place a car for him at the elevator. The railway companies refused to place cars at the elevators, consequently elevators were not used in that way. This section has been introduced into the Bill to overcome that difficulty.

I would point out to the hon. member for East Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) that a man living twenty-five miles from the railway station is not in a position to load a car from a platform, as is a man living near the railway station. When he brings his grain he has to put it in an elevator. If he is given the privilege of combining with others to ship it, I cannot see that anybody would be injured. And these are the people that require to be provided for. Very often, the first year, they have not large crops or large means. If the law can be so amended so as to secure for them three cents or four cents per bushel that they would not otherwise receive, it ought to be given them.	.

This matter was given very serious consideration by the delegates both from the Grain Dealers' Association and the Grain Growers' Association who have visited Ottawa since the commencement of this session, and who spent not only hours, but days considering the various points coming up under these amendments, and who are largely responsible for the shape in which these amendments now appear. The point raised by the hon. member for Saskatchewan was given the utmost consideration. As has been explained by the minister, an additional privilege is being given by this section. Under the amendments adopted last year the farmers did not have the privilege of ordering a car to be spotted at the elevator to be loaded direct there, but were limited, so far as direct loading is concerned, to the platforms and flat warehouses. The difficulty found in making the provision my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) suggests is this : It was recognized that this extra privilege that is being given to the farmers of loading through the elevators will open a pretty wide door for-I suppose we will have to use the word ' fraud,' through perhaps that is an extreme term-a prettywide door for fraud on the part of managers of elevators. These men may easily make arrangements with certain farmers or other people to order cars to elevators-perhaps people who do not own grain at all-simply to get for these managers more cars to load than they are entitled to. In later provisions of this Bill, it will be seen that very strict regulation is made with regard to the

distribution of cars. The principle of first come first served is endeavoured to be followed in this amendment, as in the case of the amendments adopted last year. My hon. friend was at some of the meetings, with myself and other North-west members, that were held in this city by the delegates I speak of. Personally I quite appreciate the disadvantage accruing to these farmers who do not grow as much grain as a carload, and f would be pleased if some reasonable suggestion could be made to their advantage. But up to the present time I have been unable, and the delegates were unable to agree upon any suggestion to give to the farmers the additional advantage, those of them who do not grow as much as a carload of wheat, without leaving the door open for an abuse of the privilege which is being granted to other farmers who do grow more than a carload of wheat, and who will be able to take advantage of the amendment.

I do not understand the arguments of the hon. gentleman. He says the door has been opened to a certain extent by allowing farmers the right to ship from the elevator. If you are opening the door by allowing a man who has a carload of wheat to come in and ship out of the elevator, what difference is it going to make if you let three men put their wheat together, and to ship it as a carload ? Where will you draw the line ? If the object is to shut off fraud by not allowing elevator men to get more cars than they are entitled to, you give them as much opportunity for fraud when you give the right to get a car for one man who has a carload of wheat as for three men combined who have a carload. The only difference is that you are protecting the poor man as against the elevator man.
The elevator men do not put any farmer in that position, because he still has the safeguard of the flat warehouse and the loading platform.

As a matter of fact, the principle was introduced of allowing grain to be shipped through elevators in order to protect people a. long distance from the railway. As the Act stood before, the only people that could take advantage of it were those living within 10 or 12 miles of the railway There are many people in the North-west who live 15, 20 or 30 miles away from a railway, and as the Act stood, these people could not take advantage of it. It is' impossible for a man who has to get a car and hold it for 24 hours, to bring in his wheat 30 miles and hold that car. This was done to allow men at a distance to take advantage of this Act. The North-west Grain Growers' Association themselves proposed to give the elevators 25 per cent of the cars,, or something to that effect, on account of their having to handle grain from a distance. This was introduced to meet Mr. SCOTT.
that difficulty, but I want it to go so far as that the poor man can take * advantage of it just as well as the wholesale man who has a carload of wheat.

I had not the advantage of meeting the grain growers and the grain dealers in agreeing upon the amendments that have been proposed to this Act, but 1 do know that last grain season attempts were made, and in some cases succeeded, whereby the grain dealers were able to get men to have cars placed at the elevators for them, in cases where they merely held the grain a day or two. As I understand it, this clause is put in to prevent that sort of thing. I see later on there is a provision made for prosecuting any person that attempts to take advantage of the Act in that way. I understand that the dealers, or rather the farmers who have elevators of their own, or who were interested in farmers' elevators, wished that cars should be placed at the elevator. While I appreciate what the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) says in regard to the poor man, it is not very often that a man having three or four hundred bushels of wheat asks to have it stored, he usually sells it. It is the man that has a carload of grain that seeks to ship it himself, and if he lias not enough for a carload, it is customary for him to get enough of his neighbours to combine with him to make up a carload. Now in order to do what the hon. member fo- Saskatchewan suggests, you will need to be very careful so that a man owning an elevator will not do as some did last year, and as many would like to do, that is, to get men who possibly have sold him 200 or 300 bushels of wheat to say, I have wheat at that elevator, and for that reason I want a car. The elevator nmn believes that, and he is enabled to get cars that he would possibly not be entitled to under the provisions of the Act.

If he was going to do anything like that it would be easier for him to get one man to do it than to get three. What is the difference ? Supposing three men owned 500 bushels of wheat each, a car holds 1,500 bushels, and what is the difference whether one man has 1,500 bushels or three men, if it is all shipped out of the same car, if they are willing to put their wheat into the same car and ship it together ? One man orders the car and I do not see any objection to that. If three men who have so much grain in the elevator-and they put it together and ship it, they are open to prosecution if they want to go together and produce their receipts, why should they not be allowed to do so ? If you do not do that you are simply putting these men, who have a small quantity of wheat at the mercy of the grain dealer or the speculator. They know he cannot take advantage of the' Grain Act to get the car. The man who has a

carload can get two or three cents more fof it, and the poor man who has not got so much will get a lower price.

1 understand that my hon. friend from East Assiniboia (Mr Douglas) agrees with the views expressed by my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), and the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd), while for myself, of course, I only desire that the clause shall be satisfactory to the producers more especially. I can see that a difficulty might arise in the way suggested by the member for Macdonald. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) says that no difficulty can arise about three farmers who own wheat combining to make up a carload. No difficulty can arise when it is honestly done. If there are three bona fide farmers who have wheat in an elevator and they combine and order a car in good faith, no harm arises. That would happen in my judgment very seldom. I think, as the member for Macdonald has said that the case of a farmer who has less than a carload of wheat and puts it in an elevator is a very rare case, and it would not be likely to occur so often as to make a practical measure of relief necessary. Under any possible legislation we might provide there would be some cases which will not be adequately met. What we have to aim at in making these amendments is how best to enable the farmer to have complete freedom in shipping his grain. I confess that either way some difficulty may arise. But the cases in which the farmer would have so small a quantity of grain as less than a carload, and would have it stored in an elevator, would seem to be so few that it would be hardly necessary to make provision to meet such a case.
I am willing to admit that if a farmer knows he cannot takejidvantage of the Act he is not going to store his grain in an elevator, and he will sell his grain for whatever he can get for it.
If there is a fiat warehouse he is not at the mercy of the elevator.
I do not know how a farmer is going to be able to ship his grain from a flat warehouse.
We are talking about communities of farmers.

If a farmer knows he cannot ship it in that way he will sell it, but it does not follow that if he can use the privilege in such a way that he can take advantage of it, although if two or three were able to store their grain together they might take advantage of the Act and get a higher price for their wheat.
I would like to know whether the storage capacity has been increased since last year ?
Yes, I think it has been to a considerable extent.
I am sure the committee would like to know in what proportion, if some of our hon. friends from the west were in a position to tell us.
I have a very casual knowledge, but I should think possibly 20 per cent would represent the increase that has been made in the elevator capacity.
There has been a very large increase at Port Arthur during the last year.
I understand that the Canadian Pacific terminal elevator capacity will be almost doubled this fall as compared with last fall.
If I am not mistaken the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Cah-adian Northern will have a capacity of 15,000,000 bushels this year.

I do not see any reason why, if three farmers have a carload of grain and they have three different certificates for that amount, two of them cannot assign their certificates to one of them and he cannot ship the grain.
Is there any legislation that prevents that ?	.

The trouble is that it would create a greater difficulty in preventing the irregular dealings that have been described by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). That difficulty is going to be serious enough as the section stands, and in the event of, the adoption of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) it would be simply impossible to procure conviction and punishment of this sort of violation of the law. I say that even as the section stands the difficulty will perhaps be great, and the delegates fully recognized the fact, but they deemed the provision necessary for the reason that without it the farmers' elevators are put out of business altogether. What are known as farmers' elevators are elevators put up by communities of farmers to enable them to ship their own grain from these elevators, and under the law as it stood last year they were not able to do business. The grain-growers while deeming this a proper provision, recognized that they were opening a door to irregular dealing, to the putting up of jobs whereby an elevator manager might enter into collusion with farmers outside to get more cars than he was entitled to in the car distribution. The case of the farmers' elevators was deemed by the delegates to be so important that they considered it necessary to put in such a provision, but although they gave the fullest possible consideration to the claims of the farmers for whom the hon. member for Saskatchewan speaks, and although these

farmers had the entire sympathy of the delegates, they were not able, nor were any of the members of parliament or senators who attended the meetings of the delegates, able to suggest such a provision as would not leave the door too wide open and make it absolutely impossible to prevent irregular dealing on the part of elevator owners.

It appears that there is a good deal in what the h.on. member for Huron (Mr. McEwen) has said that if three farmers had a certain amount of wheat) in an elevator and two of them sold it to the third one, he should have a right to ship it. But, where would he come in under this Bill as you have it now ? If three men have a carload of wheat and two sell it to the third man, would the third man have the right to ship it ?
I think so.

On section 14,
Can two or more parties use that warehouse and still order cars to it ?

Yes. I movie that the words ' of not less than 3,000 bushels capacity ' be inserted Mr. SCOTT.
after the word 'warehouse.' That was in the old Act, and after full consideration it seems to me that it is not good policy to permit warehouses of less than 3,000 bushels capacity. Every member of the House whom I have spoken to on the subject agraes to that view.

I am bound to say that I do not approve of this suggestion. I do not think that we ought to commence travelling backwards in the way of restrictions, and last year it was the opinion of the North-west members and a very large majority of the people who advised them, that the old restriction with regard to the size of the flat warehouses should be removed. It was removed, and for my part I certainly do not approve of reenacting it. So far as I know, there is no person in a position to make a complaint of the operation of last year's Act with that restriction removed. The question, of granaries was raised by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to-night, and it is a question that is very generally mentioned when we are dealing with grain blockades or any matter connected with the grain trade. I have before pointed out in this House that a farmer in the prairie country who is going to do his business to the best advantage cannot afford to have his granary on his farm, if his farm is far removed from the railway. He is bound to have his storage space right beside the railway in order that he may be at the best advantage. The provision for the flat warehouses as the Act was amended last year enabled any farmer, no matter what his output, to store his grain on the railway track, and those farmers, who were championed by my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) to-night, are those who are chiefly affected by this amendment. A farmer who grows 1,500 or 2,000 bushels of grain was permitted by the Act of last year to build his granary beside the railway, and that privilege enabled him to do his business most advantageously.

Do you know of any flat warehouses that have been erected of less than 3,000 bushels capacity ?
Mi-. SCOTT. Not that I am aware of.

I am quite certain that I never saw one and I am quite sure that my hon. friend (ill-. Scott) will never see one whether this law is changed or not. It seems to me that to give authority by an Act of parliament to require a railway company to give a site for a warehouse to hold grain of less than 3,000 bushels capacity, is an absurdity Suppose they started to erect small granaries of 1,000 bushels capacity, these would string out along the railway and fill up the sidings, and while it might be convenient for the farmers who happened to get in

first, it would be a great inconvenience to c the general public, and would impede the < shipment of grain and generally congest [DOT] the business. The best proof that this is a sound view is that although under last year's Act there was no restriction, these small warehouses were not put up, because it would not pay, under the circumstances, to erect them. It may not be absolutely essential that there should be a limit, but it seems to hie that the limit suggested is a reasonable one, and that it would be wise to insert such a provision.

When I come to think of it, X believe I can give the hon. minister instances of warehouses that have been erected of less than 3,000 bushels capacity'. In Balgonie, McLean, Qu'Appelle, Indian Head, Sintaluta, and other points, there were last year and the year before scores of granaries put up by farmers for the purpose of getting their grain stored beside the railway track while the roads were passable. While I am not positive about the size of these granaries, I am pretty certain that scores of them put up at these towns were of a capacity of less than 3.000 bushels. My impression is that the average was 1,200 or 1,500 bushels capacity, and some of them -were put right on tlid railway company's premises alongside of the track to save the necessity of more frequent handling than would otherwise be required.

I noticed myself in the riding of my hon. friend from Bast Assini-boia some of these so-called warehouses stretched out along the track and built something like a box car with a little round roof. If you are going to allow' every man in the country to build one of these things on the railw'ay premises around the station, I do not know how people are going to do business. The law requires them to cover them w'ith metal, and that I suppose prevented them from building on the railyvay premises before. If a man wants to build a flat warehouse, if it is not going to hold 3,000 bushels of grain, he should not be allow'ed to build it on the railroad.

I think the hon. member for West Assiniboia forgets that most of these temporary warehouses in my constituency are on sidings. This section requires them to be on a siding or on some sw'itch in connection with the railway. Most of these temporary granaries may be on the railway property, but they are not on the track or on a sw'itch. I should not oppose the utmost freedom. In the Bill of last year everything in the shape of a restriction was removed, and very largely at my suggestion ; but I dislike very much to' compel a railway company to provide such a number of sites on a common switch as might be in requisition. A building holding 3,000 bushels is a small building. I know that from personal experience, having built temporary granaries, and having shift-251
ed them from one part of the farm to another. Did I contemplate building a flat warehouse and asking that a site on a sw'itch should be furnished by the railw'ay'^ company, I w'ould not for a moment think of putting up a building that would] hold less than 3,000 bushels. Some phraseology might be adopted leaving it largely to the discretion of the grain commissioner to determine the size of the building.

My own impression is that the railway company has very little to fear so long as we leave the restriction, w'hich was the only one left last year, providing that the flat warehouse must be covered w'ith metal. So far as I know', no complaint has been made on the part of the railway company that any person has built a flat warehouse and covered it with metal, of less than 3,000 bushels capacity. It is well known that a majority of these warehouses were not on the railway, simply because of that restriction. It would be a great advantage to those farmers who are compelled to haul their grain or leave it .on the farm until the road breaks up in the spring, to have the granaries on the sidings. It would save them an extra haul.

boundary between British Columbia and the North-west Territories.' On section 62,

I want to move another clause, and I think this is the proper place to propose it. I will read it :
These commissioners .shall semi-daily, as soon as possible after nine o'clock in the morning and twelve o'clock noon, on every day between the 31st day of August in each year and the first day of April t'he following year communicate by telegraph to the railway station agent at places in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories where grain elevators are situated, the price of No. 1 Manitoba hard wheat and of No. 1 Northern wheat at Fort William, at the said respective hours, and each such agent shall immediately after the receipt of such telegram publish the same by writing it legibly on a blacboard in a convenient place accessible to the public at such station.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that if this was done, I think, it would to a great extent do away with much of this trouble that we have had as regards the loading of cars and the loading platforms.
I understand that such a provision prevails in certain states of the union, and it has worked very acceptably. It is true there will be some difficulty in carrying it out, but there should be none, for the reason that in several of the towns In Manitoba and the North-west Territories the price of grain in Minneapolis and Chicago is telegraphed every half hour. Now if the farmer could go to the station and ascertain the price of these grades of wheat at Fort William, at nine o'clock in the morning and at one o'clock in the afternoon, he would know exactly what price he is receiving for his wheat, and what rate the elevator pan or the track buyer is allowing him for it and what profit he is receiving. Then if he is satisfied with the profit that the grain dealer is allowing him he can sell him his wheat, if he is not satisfied with it he can ask for a car and ship it. I think if this system was adopted it would to a great extent do away with a great deal of trouble

we have had in the past with regard to this phase of the question. I brought this matter up before the minister last year and he requested me not to press it. I was not aware this matter was being brought up tonight, and in order to give him notice of it, I handed this motion to the clerk.

I think there is something to be said in favour of the suggestion that the hon. gentleman has made. The difficulty is in carrying it out. If I remember aright, the objection which obtained in my mind to this proposition when it was made before, was in regard to the commissioner taking the responsibility of deciding what the prices were and sending them out, because the probability is that the community at large would regard the commissioner as being responsible for these prices, and in cases of dispute as to accuracy, no doubt the department would be held responsible. There may be some way to work out the plan which my hon. friend has suggested. I have not given the subject any special consideration since the matter was before the House on a former occasion. But there is this to be said against it, that while the matter has been discussed and while every conceivable phase of the Grain Act has been discussed during the last year very fully by the grain growers who certainly do not lack full knowledge of the situation and the difficulties that they have encountered up to the present time, I believe none of them have suggested that this particular provision should be inserted in the Act. However, I am quite willing that it should receive proper consideration and I will allow the matter to stand over, if my hon. friend agrees to that view. I will leave the Bill in committee, think it over in the course of the next three or four days and get such information as I can upon the subject. I will ask the opinion of the commissioner as to whether he thinks it practicable or not and bring it before the committee again at a later day.

I was endeavouring to assist my hon. friend from Macdonald in regard to drafting something that would cover the case, but I do not know whether it is in proper form, as it has been done very hastily. There may be some difficulty in this matter if the commissioner is not at some particular point all the time. Is the commissioner stationed in any particular point, or does he move around the country ?

No, he is not at any particular point, but that difficulty could be got over in this way: He has an office in Winnipeg, and he has an assistant there, and, of course, the prices are quoted there every hour of the day. There would be no difficulty from that standpoint, because his assistant could send out the prices as well as he could himself.
251J

The difficulty that the hon. minister speaks of as regards the question of liability would be a very serious one, and if the proposition of my hon. friend from Macdonald were adopted it would be very desirable to add, to the clause which has been drafted, some provision to the effect that neither the commissioner nor the government should be in any way responsible for mistakes, because mistakes sometimes occur in the transmission of messages. There will be no possibility of any wilful mistake, but it might occur, as the hon. minister says, in the transmission of the message or from wrong information received by the commissioner.

I do not think there is a very serious practical difficulty, with all due deference to my hon. friend from Macdonald. Some years ago, undoubtedly, farmers did suffer from lack of knowledge as to what was the price of grain, but I do not think it can be said at the present time that they have any difficulty in finding out what grain is selling for. When they come into town or come to a station, they have no difficulty in finding out what grain is selling for. The railway station agent is there and he gets the information, and there is nearly always more than one buyer. Still, I will go into it and see what can be done, if anything, to meet the wishes of the hon. gentleman.

I think the hon. minister is mistaken in regard to that, because I know that there are times when as much as 10 cents a bushel was made by grain men in handling wheat. If the farmers knew what the price of wheat was, knowing the freight to Fort William, they would get cars under circumstances of that Kind, ship themselves, and the dealers could not treat them in that way. The hon. minister says that farmers have no difficulty in ascertaining the price. The dealers themselves know the price. They get it from their houses every morning and every day at noon, and if the dealers can get that information there is no reason why the farmers should not have it from the commissioner. I have thought a great deal upon the subject, and I believe it would be a great benefit to the people of the North-west Territories, and I think if the hon. minister gives it as much attention as I have he will see that it is possible to provide for it.

If it is such a benefit as the hon. member for Macdonald says, how is it that the delegates of the Grain Grower's' Association sent down here by the farmers did not advocate it ? They never made any suggestion in that direction, and 1 think they can be pretty well trusted to look after the interests of the farmers in a matter of that kind.

I do no think that all the wisdom in the North-west Territories was

confined to the three or four grain growers who were sent down here. I have had opportunities of discussing this question with a great many farmers in the west, and they have expressed a desire to have such a provision as I have suggested.

The Grain Growers' Association represents the farmers of all parts of the North-west Territories. All the amendments to the Act that they desired were discussed, and when the delegates came down here representing the farmers, if they had required this amendment they would have asked for it.
Probably if I had had an opportunity of discussing the question with them, that no doubt, the hon. member for Saskatchewan had, this amendment might have been engrafted on the Bill.
They were here for a week.
I was not invited to take part in their meetings.
Neither was I.

I was going to suggest that the hon. member for Macdonald probably had not an opportunity of bringing this before the representatives of the association, and that the hon. member for Saskatchewan, knowing that the hon. member for Macdonald had brought the matter up last year, in all probability overlooked or intentionally neglected to bring it to the attention of the delegates. I remember that this question was discussed here last year, and I "thought the idea put forward by tlie hon. member for Macdonald an excellent one. It seems to me to be a grand thing that the farmers in the North-west should be able to get information not only once a day, but at all hours of the day as to the price at which grain is selling at Fort William or Winnipeg, or at leading points, so that he will know that he is not; being taken advantage of. I am quite sure that the hon. minister can make provision for this, and I think the people of the North-west will be very much indebted to the hon. member for Macdonald for bringing this matter up.
Mr. SCOTT If my recollection is right this is not the suggestion that was made by the hon. member for Macdonald last year. I think he suggested last year that the railway companies should be compelled to 'furnish this information at every shipping point. This is a point that was not overlooked by the delegates from the Grain Growers' Association. It was discussed by them at various meetings, but was not pressed. They appeared to take the view that it was an unnecessary provision to add to the Act. I do not know what the custom, or practice, or system, may be which is prevailing in Manitoba, but in my own section of the North-west Territories the farmers themselves have taken steps to possess themselves daily of the information from Winnipeg or Fort William. As a matter of fact, the information comes from Winnipeg. They have certain arrangements made by which they are advised from time to time, sometimes more than once a day, when changes take place in the price. These delegates did not appear to wish that such a provision should be added to the Bill.
